heroHeadline: SCOTUS Conservative Majority Signals Against Haitian TPS; GSF Transition Exposes Security Gap as Kenya MSS Formally Ends
heroSubtitle: On April 29, 2026, the US Supreme Court's conservative 6-3 majority appeared strongly inclined to side with the Trump administration in Noem v. Doe / Trump v. Miot, signaling that federal courts may have no power to review TPS termination decisions — a ruling expected by late June or early July 2026 that would threaten deportation proceedings for approximately 350,000 Haitian TPS holders and disruption to 87,000 US-born children of TPS holders. Haitian diaspora community leaders report widespread fear and financial paralysis; Haitian TPS holders contribute nearly $6 billion to the US economy annually per CNN Business. Separately, Kenya's final 150 MSS officers departed Haiti on April 28, 2026, formally ending the 22-month Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission established under UN Security Council Resolution 2699. The withdrawal leaves Haiti's security transition in the hands of the Gang Suppression Force advance contingent of approximately 545 personnel — 400 Chadian troops, 75 Guatemalan police, and 70 Salvadoran police — conducting joint operations with the Haitian National Police while the full 5,500-person GSF works toward operational capacity projected for fall–end 2026. Gang control of Port-au-Prince expanded from approximately 80% to approximately 90% of the capital during the MSS mission's 22-month lifespan. Haiti's 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan remains critically underfunded at approximately 20% of the $880 million needed, with 5.8 million Haitians (52% of the population) facing IPC Phase 3+ food insecurity and 600,000 in Phase 5 famine conditions; WFP warns it may be forced to cut 1 million people from food assistance by June 2026 without emergency contributions.
